passages.t: Leviathan slain, and a vineyard sung again
passages.happening:
‘In that day the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent’ (verse 1), the coiling serpent, and he will slay the dragon of the sea.

In that day, sing about a fruitful vineyard (verse 2). ‘I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it’ (verse 3). God is not angry. If thorns and briers stood against him, he would trample and burn them (verse 4). Or let them come to him for protection and make peace with him (verse 5).

‘In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes chapters 24 to 27. The section began with the earth laid waste and ends with Israel's exiles gathered to worship, so it moves from judgment on the world to worship.

Leviathan was not invented by Israel. Clay tablets found at Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BC, tell how the storm god Baal defeated a sea monster called Lotan, described with the same phrases Isaiah uses: the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent, with seven heads. Israel's poets used that well-known figure for the forces of chaos and the enemy powers behind the nations. Isaiah does not treat Leviathan as a rival god. The LORD simply kills it with his sword, and the whole battle takes one verse.

The vineyard of chapter 5 returns transformed. There the LORD abandoned his vineyard to thorns because it gave only sour grapes. Here he guards it night and day, waters it, and it fills the world with fruit. Even the thorns are offered peace. The first hearers, who knew the first vineyard song, would hear the reversal.
passages.later: A psalm sings, ‘You crushed the heads of Leviathan’ (Psalm 74:14). Job is asked, ‘Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook’ (Job 41:1). And Revelation pictures ‘the great dragon’, ‘that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan’, hurled down (Revelation 12:9).
passages.asks: The vineyard that once gave sour grapes is now guarded and watered night and day. Ask where God has given you a second chance after a season of bad fruit. And ask what it means that even the thorns are invited to make peace with him.

passages.t: Punishment measured, and idols crushed to chalk
passages.happening:
‘Has the LORD struck Israel as He struck her oppressors? Was she killed like those who slayed her?’ (verse 7). By war and exile God contended with her and drove her away with a fierce wind (verse 8).

‘Therefore Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for’ (verse 9), and the fruit of the removal of his sin will be this: he makes all the altar stones like crushed chalk, and no Asherah poles or incense altars remain standing.

The fortified city lies deserted, a homestead abandoned, where calves graze and strip the branches (verse 10). When the branches dry, they are broken off and used for kindling, ‘for this is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
God's dealing with Israel is measured. He struck Israel, but not as he struck her oppressors. Exile was meant to purge, not to destroy.

Asherah poles were wooden objects for the goddess Asherah, often set up beside altars at local shrines. Destroying them was the mark of real reform, as when Hezekiah broke them down. Crushing altar stones to chalk meant no shrine could be rebuilt from them. The proof of forgiveness is a people who no longer want their idols.

The fortified city of verse 10 is hard to identify. Some take it as the oppressor's city; others as Samaria or Jerusalem under judgment, since verse 11 speaks of a people without understanding. The context of verses 7 to 11, about Israel's own punishment, makes an Israelite city possible, but interpreters remain divided.
passages.later: Kings tells how Hezekiah ‘removed the high places, shattered the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles’ (2 Kings 18:4). And Paul, writing of Israel's future, quotes the promise, ‘And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins’ (Romans 11:27).
passages.asks: Forgiveness shows itself when the idols are crushed and not rebuilt. Ask what idols you have set aside but kept the stones of, just in case. And ask whether you believe God's discipline in your life is measured, not destroying.

passages.t: Gathered one by one, and a great horn
passages.happening:
‘In that day the LORD will thresh from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one’ (verse 12).

‘And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Threshing separated grain from stalks by beating, and gathering one by one describes a careful harvest where nothing is lost. God will not lose a single one of his scattered people.

The shofar, a ram's horn, was blown to call assemblies, sound alarms and announce holy days. Its blast here summons the scattered people home.

On the traditional view, the exiles in Assyria and Egypt fit the deportations Assyria carried out from the northern kingdom, especially after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, and the Israelites who fled to Egypt. On a later dating, the verse reflects the scattered Jewish communities of the Persian period in Mesopotamia and in Egypt. The borders of verse 12, from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, are the ideal borders of the land promised to Abraham, not the borders Judah held in either period. They make no claim about any border today.
passages.later: God had promised Abram land ‘from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates’ (Genesis 15:18). Jesus speaks of the gathering at the end: ‘He will send out His angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather His elect from the four winds’ (Matthew 24:31).
passages.asks: God will gather his people one by one, so that none is lost. Ask whether you believe you are known to God by name. And ask who is scattered from your own community that you would want to see gathered home.
